segments.text: Inevitably, in this life, we are subject to emotions.
Some of the emotions are pleasant.
There's friendliness, love, compassion, gratitude, joy, delight.
And some of the emotions are unpleasant.
We are subject to anger, fear, sadness, hurt, frustration, jealousy, embarrassment, shame, guilt, impatience.
When we encounter the difficult emotions, that is to say the unpleasant emotions,
our tendency is to become preoccupied with two things.
One is figuring out what's going on, and the other is doing something about what's going on.

And this is completely legitimate. Our thinking mind has a job to do, which is consider situations, consider circumstances, figure out, is it them? Is it me? Why am I going through this? What caused this situation? That's quite legitimate.
And then we have to do things. We have to express ourselves, take actions, say things.
So, whenever we encounter these negative or difficult emotions,
immediately we're drawn into the aspect of figuring things out and dealing with the circumstance.
The problem is twofold.
The first is that often the difficult emotion gets in the way of clear thinking and clear action.

It will turn into a problem.
Maybe big, maybe small.

It distorts our perception, and it makes it difficult for us to think.
So often, when we encounter a difficult emotion, we experience a lot of confusion.

That's the first problem.
The second problem is that our tendency is to get involved only in a consideration of the circumstances and what we should do about them.
